title: Raspberry Pi 5 against Pi 4
subtitle: Is the upgrade worth it? A spec-by-spec scorecard from the product briefs

scenes.narration: The Raspberry Pi five is out, and plenty of people still run a Pi four. So is the upgrade worth it?
scenes.question: Is the upgrade worth it?
scenes.note: Every number here is from Raspberry Pi’s own product briefs

steps.say: Every number in this video comes from the two boards’ official product briefs. No rumours.

scenes.title: Spec by spec
scenes.narration: Let’s go down the spec sheet one row at a time, and give each row to whichever board wins it.

steps.say: The processor. The Pi five has a newer core, the A seventy six, and runs it at 2.4 gigahertz instead of 1.8. First point goes to the five.
Graphics and memory both go to the five as well: a new graphics chip that runs Vulkan, newer memory, and up to sixteen gigabytes of it.
The two camera and display ports are now twice as wide, and each one takes either a camera or a screen.
USB and networking are the same on both. That one is a tie.
Power is where the four wins. The five wants a five amp supply, so your old 3 amp charger may not cut it.
The five is rated to run hotter, up to 70 degrees, and it will be made for two years longer. Final score, 6 to 1.

scenes.title: Processor speed, as times the Pi 4
scenes.narration: Now the big one. How much faster is it, really? Start with both boards at the same height.

steps.say: The clock alone is 2.4 against 1.8. That makes it only a third faster.
But each tick of the newer core gets more done. Raspberry Pi says the five is at least twice as fast.
And up to three times, depending on the job. That is their number, not a test we ran, but most of it comes from the core, not the clock.

draw.write:
mostly the newer core,
not the clock

scenes.title: Things only the Pi 5 has
scenes.narration: Then there are the things the Pi four simply does not have.

rows.label: Clock that keeps time when off
PCI Express, for fast drives
cells: One lane, with an add-on board

rows.label: Its own input and output chip

steps.say: A power button. Finally. No more pulling the cable out.
A real time clock, so it knows the time even after it was switched off, if you add a little battery.
A PCI Express slot. With an add-on board you can plug in a fast solid state drive instead of booting from a memory card.
And a chip Raspberry Pi designed itself, which handles most of the plugs and pins, and more than doubles the USB speed overall.

scenes.title: List price in US dollars, by memory size
scenes.narration: So what does it cost? Here are the list prices for the memory sizes both boards come in.

steps.say: At one gigabyte, the five is 10 dollars more.
At two and four gigabytes, also ten dollars more.
And at eight gigabytes, ten dollars again. On a 165 dollar board that is only about six percent.

scenes.note: for two to three times the speed, by Raspberry Pi’s count
items: Want a desktop, a fast drive or two cameras? Upgrade
Pi 4 already doing its job? Keep it
Upgrading? Budget for a 5 A power supply

steps.say: If you are buying a new board, the extra ten dollars is easily worth it. Get the five.
If you want a small desktop, a fast drive, or two cameras, upgrade.
But if your Pi four already runs your home server just fine, there is no need to throw it out.
And if you do upgrade, plan on a bigger power supply.
